                                                   Subgroups of free groups with the same commutator subgroup

                                                                                   TURSUNBAEV ARTUR


                                                 Abstract. We prove that any two subgroups of a free group with the same nontrivial commuta-
                                                 tor subgroup are equal.This yields an affirmative answer to Shpilrain’s Problem F15: normality
                                                 of [R, R] in a free group F implies normality of the noncyclic subgroup R. No restrictions on
                                                 ranks or indices are imposed.
arXiv:2609.06755v1 [math.GR] 6 Sep 2026




                                                                                    1. Introduction
                                             In 1990, V. E. Shpilrain posed, in the 11th edition of The Kourovka Notebook, the question of
                                          whether normality of the commutator subgroup of a noncyclic subgroup of a free group implies
                                          normality of the subgroup itself; see [7, Problem 11.124]. This question was subsequently restated
                                          as Problem F15 in the book by Kapovich, Myasnikov, and Shpilrain [6, Problem F15, p. 10].
                                             The motivation comes from the classical Auslander–Lyndon theorem: if N and M are normal
                                          subgroups of a nonabelian free group and N ′ ≤ M ′ , then N ≤ M . The normality assumption
                                          is essential here: Dunwoody [5, p. 153] constructed subgroups N, M ≤ F such that M ◁ F ,
                                          N ′ ≤ M ′ , but N ≰ M . Thus, the normality assumption on N cannot simply be omitted from
                                          the Auslander–Lyndon theorem.
                                             In this context, Shpilrain’s problem has the following precise formulation: if F is a noncyclic
                                          free group, R ≤ F is a noncyclic subgroup, and
                                                                                            R′ ◁ F,
                                          must we have
                                                                                            R ◁ F?
                                            In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative. Throughout, we use the convention
                                                                           [a, b] = a−1 b−1 ab,        H ′ = [H, H].
                                          Theorem 1.1. Let F be a free group of arbitrary rank, and let H, K ≤ F . If
                                                                                        H ′ = K ′ ̸= 1,
                                          then H = K.
                                          Corollary 1.2 (F15). Let F be a free group, and let R ≤ F be a noncyclic subgroup. Then
                                                                                  R′ ◁ F     =⇒        R ◁ F.
                                          Derivation of the corollary from the theorem. The subgroup R is free and noncyclic, so R′ =
                                                                                                                                    ̸ 1.
                                          For every f ∈ F , normality of R′ gives
                                                                                (f −1 Rf )′ = f −1 R′ f = R′ .
                                          Theorem 1.1 implies f −1 Rf = R. Hence R ◁ F .                                                          □
                                            Another immediate consequence of the main theorem is the equality
                                                                                     NF (H ′ ) = NF (H)
                                          for every noncyclic subgroup H of a free group F .
                                             The main theorem can also be formulated as the assertion that the map
                                                                                           H 7−→ H ′
                                          is injective on the set of subgroups H ≤ F with H ′ ̸= 1.
                                                                                               1
                    2. Classical results and the finite-index case
Proposition 2.1 (Auslander–Lyndon). Let E be a noncyclic free group.
   (a) If 1 ̸= N ◁ E, then the action of E/N on N/N ′ by conjugation is faithful. In other words,
       if g ∈ E and [N, g] ≤ N ′ , then g ∈ N .
   (b) If N1 , N2 ◁ E and N1′ ≤ N2′ , then N1 ≤ N2 . In particular, N1′ = N2′ implies N1 = N2 .
  These are Theorems 1 and 3 of [1, pp. 929 and 931], respectively. Neither statement requires
the rank to be finite.
Lemma 2.2. Let E be a noncyclic free group, and let H ≤ E satisfy [E : H] < ∞ and D = H ′ ◁E.
Then H ◁ E.
Proof. Set                          \
                  C = coreE (H) =         g −1 Hg,         Ω = E/C,           P = H/C.
                                    g∈E
The group Ω is finite. Normality of D and the inclusion D ≤ H imply D ≤ C. Hence C ′ ≤ D ≤ C.
  All modules in this proof are right modules. Consider
                         V = (C/C ′ ) ⊗ Q,           W = (D/C ′ ) ⊗ Q ≤ V.
Conjugation defines a right QΩ-module structure on V , and normality of D makes W a submodule.
For a subgroup B ≤ Ω, let IB denote the augmentation ideal of QB.
  The five-term exact sequence in homology [3, p. 47] for the extension C ◁ H yields an exact
sequence
                       H2 (P ; Q) −→ VP −→ H1 (H; Q) −→ H1 (P ; Q) −→ 0.
Since P is finite, both outer homology terms vanish, giving an isomorphism
                                   VP = V /V IP ∼
                                                = H1 (H; Q).
The kernel of the homomorphism C/C ′ → H/H ′ is
                                     (C ∩ H ′ )/C ′ = D/C ′ .
Since Q is a flat Z-module, the kernel of the natural map V → H1 (H; Q) is W . On the other
hand, by the preceding isomorphism, this kernel is V IP . Therefore,
                                             W = V IP .                                     (2.1)
  We show that V contains a direct QΩ-summand isomorphic to QΩ. Indeed, if rank E = n < ∞,
the relation module exact sequence for C ◁ E has the form
                               0 −→ V −→ (QΩ)n −→ IΩ −→ 0.
A more general form of this sequence can be found, for example, in Blackburn [4, p. 470].
  The semisimplicity of QΩ and the decomposition QΩ ∼   = Q ⊕ IΩ give
                                     V ∼= Q ⊕ (QΩ)n−1 .
Here n ≥ 2. If rank E = ∞, choose a finite subset of a free basis whose images generate Ω, and
one further basis element x. Replacing x by xw−1 for a suitable word w in the chosen finite
subset yields a free basis X of E containing an element x ∈ C.
  For this basis, the relation module exact sequence has the form
                                             ∂
                                  M
                      0 −→ V −→       ey QΩ −
                                            → IΩ −→ 0,       ∂(ey ) = ȳ − 1.
                                 y∈X

Since x ∈ C, we have ∂(ex ) = 0, and hence
                                                                       
                                                          M
                              V = ex QΩ ⊕ V ∩                     ey QΩ .
                                                         y∈X\{x}

Thus, in this case as well, V contains a direct QΩ-summand isomorphic to QΩ.
                                                     2
  In either case, choose a direct summand U ∼
                                            = QΩ and write
                                               V = U ⊕ U0 .
Let π : V → U denote the corresponding QΩ-linear projection. By (2.1), we obtain
                                π(W ) = π(V IP ) = π(V )IP = U IP .
Since W is a QΩ-submodule, its image U IP is stable under right multiplication by elements
of Ω. Under the identification U ∼ = QΩ, it follows that J = QΩIP is also stable under right
multiplication by elements of Ω.
   As a Q-vector space, QΩ/J has a basis indexed by the left cosets ωP . Indeed, J is spanned by
all differences ωp − ω, where ω ∈ Ω and p ∈ P . For p ∈ P and ω ∈ Ω, stability of J under right
multiplication by elements of Ω gives
                                            (p − 1)ω ∈ J,
whence
                                    pωP = ωP,            ω −1 pω ∈ P.
Thus P ◁ Ω, and hence H ◁ E.                                                                     □

                                3. Chains in Schreier graphs
  Fix a free basis X of the free group E. For H ≤ E, let ΓH denote the Schreier graph with
vertices Hg and positively oriented edges
                                           x
                                      Hg −
                                         → Hgx,             x ∈ X.
For an oriented edge e, let o(e) and t(e) denote its initial and terminal vertices, respectively.
  See the classical exposition of the Reidemeister–Schreier method in [2, §2.3].
  Every word w over the alphabet X ±1 determines a unique path starting at each vertex of ΓH .
Reading a fixed word defines a permutation of the vertex set of ΓH .
  Let w ∈ H. The corresponding path starting at the vertex H is closed. Let
                                         σH (w) ∈ C1 (ΓH ; Z)
denote its 1-chain, where C1 (ΓH ; Z) is the free abelian group on the positively oriented edges of
ΓH . The coefficient of an edge in σH (w) is the number of times it is traversed in the positive
direction minus the number of times it is traversed in the opposite direction. Free reduction of
the word does not change this chain.
   For u, v ∈ H, we have
                                    σH (uv) = σH (u) + σH (v),
so this defines a homomorphism
                                      σH : H −→ C1 (ΓH ; Z).
  The standard identification
                                           π1 (ΓH , H) ∼
                                                       =H
and passage to the abelianization give
                                               ker σH = H ′ .                                 (3.1)
Indeed, since ΓH is a graph,
                               H1 (ΓH ; Z) = Z1 (ΓH ; Z) ⊆ C1 (ΓH ; Z),
a closed path has zero homology class if and only if its associated 1-chain is zero.
Lemma 3.1 (On a central coset). Let H ≤ E, D = H ′ ◁ E, and suppose that there exists
c ∈ H \ D such that
                                      cD ∈ Z(E/D).
Then [E : H] < ∞. More precisely, for any word of length ℓ representing c with respect to the
basis X, we have [E : H] ≤ ℓ.
                                                     3
Proof. For every g ∈ E, we have
                                        gcg −1 c−1 ∈ D = H ′ .
Thus gcg −1 ∈ H, and the path corresponding to the word c and starting at the vertex Hg is
closed. The path in ΓH corresponding to the word gcg −1 and starting at H has the form
                                                g · c · g −1 ,
where the chains of the segments g and g −1 cancel each other.
  Moreover, gcg −1 and c have the same image in H/H ′ . Consequently, the chain of the closed
path corresponding to the word c and starting at an arbitrary vertex Hg is
                                            α = σH (c) ̸= 0.
                                    / H ′ and (3.1).
The fact that α ̸= 0 follows from c ∈
  Fix a positively oriented edge e whose coefficient in α is nonzero. Since the chain of every closed
path corresponding to the word c is α, each such path traverses e in one of the two directions.
  Write
                                    c = s1 · · · sℓ ,        sj ∈ X ±1 ,
and set uj−1 = s1 · · · sj−1 . Let the edge e be labeled by x ∈ X. If the j-th step of the path
starting at a vertex v traverses e in the positive direction, then sj = x and
                                             vuj−1 = o(e).

If e is traversed in the opposite direction, then sj = x−1 and
                                             vuj−1 = t(e).
Consequently,
         V (ΓH ) ⊆ { o(e)u−1                                 −1
                          j−1 : 1 ≤ j ≤ ℓ, sj = x } ∪ { t(e)uj−1 : 1 ≤ j ≤ ℓ, sj = x
                                                                                    −1
                                                                                       }.

Thus, each j corresponds to at most one initial vertex, and hence
                                      [E : H] = |V (ΓH )| ≤ ℓ.
                                                                                                   □


                                  4. Intersection dichotomy
Lemma 4.1. Let H, K ≤ F and H ′ = K ′ = D ̸= 1. Then
                                  H=K            or         H ∩ K = D.
Proof. The subgroup D is normal in both H and K, so
                                          D ◁ E := ⟨H, K⟩.
  Suppose that there exists c ∈ (H ∩ K) \ D. The subgroups H/D and K/D are abelian and
generate E/D. Since cD belongs to both, it centralizes H/D and K/D, and hence
                                            cD ∈ Z(E/D).
  Lemma 3.1, applied to H ≤ E and K ≤ E, gives
                                  [E : H] < ∞,              [E : K] < ∞.
By Lemma 2.2, both subgroups are normal in E. Then Proposition 2.1(b), applied to H, K ◁ E,
gives H = K.
                      ̸ K, then H ∩ K ⊆ D. The reverse inclusion is clear, so H ∩ K = D. □
   Consequently, if H =

 5. Finiteness of the family of subgroups with a common commutator subgroup
Lemma 5.1. Let D ≤ F and d ∈ D \ D′ . Then there exists a finite set T ⊂ F \ D with the
following property:
                    D ≤ H ≤ F, H ∩ T = ∅ =⇒ d ∈          / H ′.                    (5.1)
Proof. Fix a free basis X of F and choose a word representing d. The corresponding closed path
in ΓD starting at the vertex D has a nonzero 1-chain σD (d) by (3.1).
   Let
                                        Db1 , . . . , Dbm
be all the distinct vertices of this path; for each of them, choose a representative bi among the
prefixes of the chosen word. Set
                                T = { bi b−1
                                          j : 1 ≤ i, j ≤ m, i ̸= j }.

Since the cosets Db1 , . . . , Dbm are pairwise distinct, we have
                                             T ∩ D = ∅.
   Let D ≤ H and H ∩ T = ∅. The natural map
                                  p : ΓD −→ ΓH ,       Dg 7−→ Hg,
is injective on the vertices of the chosen path: the equality Hbi = Hbj would imply bi b−1
                                                                                        j ∈ H,
contradicting H ∩ T = ∅.
   Let
                                   p# : C1 (ΓD ; Z) −→ C1 (ΓH ; Z)
denote the induced homomorphism on 1-chains.
   The map p is also injective on the positively oriented edges occurring in the chosen path.
Indeed, both endpoints of each such edge belong to the chosen set of vertices, and a positively
oriented edge of a Schreier graph is uniquely determined by its initial vertex and label. Since
p preserves labels and orientations, distinct edges in the support of σD (d) have distinct images.
Therefore,
                                     σH (d) = p# σD (d) ̸= 0.
                      / H ′.
By (3.1), we obtain d ∈                                                                        □
Lemma 5.2. For every nontrivial subgroup D ≤ F , the set
                                    R(D) = {H ≤ F : H ′ = D}
is finite.
Proof. By the Nielsen–Schreier theorem, D is free; since D ̸= 1, we have D/D′ =
                                                                              ̸ 1. Choose
d ∈ D \ D′ and a finite set T as in Lemma 5.1.
  If H ∈ R(D), then D = H ′ ≤ H and d ∈ H ′ . By (5.1), we have H ∩ T ̸= ∅.
  If H, K ∈ R(D) and H =   ̸ K, then Lemma 4.1 gives H ∩ K = D. Since T ∩ D = ∅, the sets
H ∩ T , H ∈ R(D), are pairwise disjoint. Hence
                                         |R(D)| ≤ |T | < ∞.
                                                                                               □

                                6. Proof of the main theorem
Proof of Theorem 1.1. Let D = H ′ = K ′ ̸= 1. By Lemma 5.2, the family R(D) is nonempty and
finite. Set
                                         E = NF (D).
Every subgroup S ∈ R(D) is contained in E, since S normalizes its commutator subgroup S ′ = D.
The group E acts by conjugation on R(D): for g ∈ E, we have
                                      (g −1 Sg)′ = g −1 Dg = D.
                                                   5
Let                                               \
                                          L=             NE (S)
                                                S∈R(D)
be the kernel of this action. Then L ◁ E and [E : L] < ∞. Set m = [E : L]. By Lagrange’s
theorem,
                                    gm ∈ L     (g ∈ E).                            (6.1)
  Suppose that H ̸= K. Then Lemma 4.1 gives
                                              H ∩ K = D.                                            (6.2)
Choose k ∈ K \ D and set q = k m . Since K/D = K/K ′ is a free abelian group, q ∈
                                                                                / D. By (6.1),
we have
                                        q ∈ K ∩ L,        q∈
                                                           / D.                                     (6.3)
For h ∈ H, set p = hm . Then p ∈ H ∩ L. Since q ∈ L, the element q normalizes H, and hence
[p, q] ∈ H. On the other hand, p ∈ L normalizes K, and q ∈ K, so [p, q] ∈ K. By (6.2), we obtain
                                          [hm , q] = [p, q] ∈ D.
  Conjugation by q induces an automorphism α of the group
                                          A = H/D = H/H ′ .
In additive notation, the relation [hm , q] ∈ D means that
                                 mα(a) = α(ma) = ma               (a ∈ A).
Since A is a free abelian group, it is torsion-free. Thus α(a) = a for all a ∈ A, that is,
                                           [H, q] ≤ D = H ′ .                                       (6.4)
  Consider
                                          E0 = ⟨H, q⟩.
The group E0 is free and noncyclic, since H ′ ̸= 1. As q ∈ L, we have H ◁ E0 . Therefore,
Proposition 2.1(a), applied to H ◁ E0 , together with (6.4), gives q ∈ H. But q ∈ K, so (6.2)
yields q ∈ D, contradicting (6.3). Hence H = K.                                            □
Corollary 6.1 (Normalizers). For every noncyclic subgroup H of a free group F , we have
                                          NF (H ′ ) = NF (H).
Proof. The inclusion NF (H) ≤ NF (H ′ ) is clear: if g normalizes H, then
                                      g −1 H ′ g = (g −1 Hg)′ = H ′ .
If g ∈ NF (H ′ ), then
                                         (g −1 Hg)′ = H ′ ̸= 1,
and Theorem 1.1 gives g −1 Hg = H.                                                                     □
